unusual.text: REGENERATION is Moog’s word for resonance (the Minimoog calls it EMPHASIS).
There is no cutoff knob as such: FIXED CONTROL VOLTAGE is a voltage added to the control inputs, an octave per volt, so the knob and an envelope work the same way.
A fixed filter bank is rare on a synthesizer. It is closer to a graphic equaliser: the bands never move with the note, which is what makes it good at body and formant sounds.
There is no module called LFO on a Moog system. The 921 with COARSE RNG on SUB is the LFO, and it can still run at audio rate when switched back.
The attenuator inputs are half-normalled: one signal into IN 1 reaches all four attenuators until the inputs below it are used, so one source can be sent at four different levels without a multiple.
Moog modules expect S-triggers, the reverse of most synths’ gates. This switch lets the CM1A send either kind, or one of each.
A 921B has no keyboard input of its own. Its playing pitch arrives from a 921A Oscillator Driver over the 921AB LINK cable, so one 921A tunes and plays a whole chain of 921Bs at once.

Moog put the filter’s control-voltage mixing in its own module, with switches, so the sources that move the filter can be changed by flicking a rocker instead of re-patching.

limits.intro: All twenty-five modules are modelled and every jack carries its signal: both 921A drivers and their four 921B oscillators, the 921, the 904A, 904B, 914 and 923 filters, the 992 and both CP3A-O control switchers, both CP3A-M mixers, the CP35, the 961, three 911 envelopes, three 902 amplifiers and the CM1A.

items.title: The OUTPUT jacks are the app’s
items.text: The real system has no master output: you patch whatever you want to hear to a mixer or audio interface. The OUTPUT plate printed on a blank panel is that cable’s other end in this app, and is marked as not on the hardware. Both jacks go to one mono output.

items.title: Tuned to the keyboard
items.text: Every oscillator is calibrated so that 0 V plays middle C at 8’, and the CM1A gives 0 V at middle C, 1 V per octave. The hardware’s own reference (2’ = 640 Hz) is set by trimmers, and its oscillators drift as they warm up; here they are always in tune and never drift.

items.title: The CM1A’s rear button and MIDI settings
items.text: The CV range (System 55 or System 100) and the duophonic mode are set with a button on the back of the CM1A, and the MIDI channel, bend range and note range in SynthTribe. Here the CM1A is always in the System 55 range and mono: CV 2 carries the same note as CV 1. MIDI IN, MIDI THRU and USB are printed.

items.title: Levels and curves are estimates
items.text: The published ranges are used: 911 times from 2 ms to 10 s, the 904A’s three frequency ranges and the 904B’s two, the 923’s 10 Hz to 10 kHz, the 961’s 40 ms to 4 s, 902 gain with 6 V for full level. The knob curves between the ends, the 902’s exponential law (about 12 dB per volt), the Q of the 914’s bands and the corner frequencies of its low-pass and high-pass (about 100 Hz and 7 kHz), the AUX level taper and the mixer’s clipping are this app’s choices.

items.title: Sync and the 921’s clamping point
items.text: SYNC IN resets the 921B on each sharp fall of its input: STRONG every time, WEAK only when the 921B is already near the end of its own cycle. The hardware’s sync circuit is softer and depends on the input’s shape. The clamping point jumps the 921 to that point of its cycle on each trigger.
